- **ATE config:** every ATE number is read through ATE's public static getters in `com.misterd.agritechevolved.Config`, for example `Config.getPlanterBasePowerConsumption()`, the same way the Powered Planter reads them. ATE's defaults appear in this document only as worked examples. Tests may pin those defaults.
- **Logistics Networks tags:** no block in this mod may be in LN's blacklist tags (`logisticsnetwork:blacklist/block` and the item, fluid and chemical variants).

## The blocks

| Block | Job |
|---|---|
- **Free form.** The multiblock is the core plus every part block connected to it face to face, directly or through other parts. Diagonal contact doesn't connect.
- **Size cap:** at most 24 parts, not counting the core. Frames count (my call).
  - Above the cap, the multiblock doesn't form, and the core's screen says why.
  - The cap is in the server config, default 24 (my call).
- **Required parts:** at least one power block, one export block and one planter block. Fertilizer, ME and frame blocks are optional.
- **Two cores:** if the connected parts reach a second core, neither forms. The core's screen names the problem block and its position (my call).
- **Re-checking:** the core re-checks the shape when a part next to the structure is placed or broken.
- **When the shape breaks:** the planter blocks stop, but every block keeps its contents.

The guide shows three example builds from the brainstorm, saved in `mockups/layouts.html`. They're examples only, since any connected shape works:

- **Raised bed under a cloche:** corner legs, a 3x3 bed and a 3x3 glass canopy.
- **Vertical farm:** a 2x2 tower with the core on the bottom floor and floors of planter blocks above it.
- **Rosette:** one block tall. The core is in the center, the other parts take the four diagonal corners, and planter blocks extend outward in four arms.

## How a planter block grows

### Contents

The planter block's screen has four slots, all filled by hand. They can also be filled from the core's screen.

| Slot | Holds |
|---|---|
| Seed | A seed bin: up to 64 seeds of one item type. Anything a Powered Planter accepts, saplings included. See "Seed traits". |
| Soil | One soil type, up to 64. Anything in ATE's `agritechevolved:soil_modifiers` data map, including Mystical Agradditions cruxes. |
| Module 1 | One ATE module type (Speed or Yield, MK1 to MK3), up to 64. |
| Module 2 | Same as module 1. |

- There's no fertilizer slot and there are no output slots. Fertilizer comes from the fertilizer blocks, and outputs go to the export blocks or ME.

### Seed traits

| Node upgrade | Energy per tick | Items a second |
|---|---|---|
| None | 2,000 RF | 0.8 |
| Iron | 10,000 RF | 64 |
| Gold | 50,000 RF | 256 |
| Diamond | 250,000 RF | 5,120 |
| Netherite | about 2.1 billion RF | 200,000 |

- Example with ATE's defaults: a full planter block of 64 nickel seeds with 2 MK3 Speed Modules, insanium farmland and the built-in cloche.
  - **Power:** it draws 32,768 RF/t whatever the seeds' traits.
  - **Items:** with seeds that have no traits, it puts out about 24 items a second. With seeds maxed in Productive Farming's Growth and Yield, like the owner's, it puts out about 320 items a second. That's more than a gold upgrade moves.
  - **Upgrade needed:** a diamond upgrade covers up to 7 such planter blocks, and power is the limit. More than 7 needs a netherite upgrade, or more nodes on the power blocks.
- The guide has to include this table and example.

See the ME block above. AE2 and Applied Flux are compile-time-only dependencies. All code that touches them sits behind a mod-loaded check, so the mod loads without them.

- There's no Productive Farming code in the mod. Its traits work through ATE's three planter events, fired as described under "How a planter block grows".

An optional Jade plugin (my call, the lowest priority in the mod):

- On the core: formed state.
- On a planter block: growing seeds and status.

id: oritech:spawner_cage
type: block
title: Spawner Cage
---

A structural cage used in conjunction with the [spawner controller](@oritech:spawner_controller). 
The cages must be placed directly beneath the controller to create a valid spawning area.

## Sizing

The required size of the cage depends on the size of the mob being spawned. 
Specifically, the cage must be wide enough for roughly twice the mob's 
width and tall enough for its height. 

When a mob type is set in the controller, it will visually highlight the needed 
cage dimensions. If the cage is incomplete or incorrect, the spawner will 
not operate.

40	- When the shape breaks, planter blocks stop and every block keeps its contents.
41	- If a connected part is in an unloaded chunk, the multiblock pauses until the chunk loads, and the core screen says so.
42	- The core can't tell what is in an unloaded chunk, so a multiblock built against the edge of the loaded area also pauses until the next chunk loads, even when no part is in it.
43	
44	## How a planter block grows
45	
46	- Growing seeds G is the smaller of the seed count and the soil count. Seeds past that stay idle.
47	- One module covers one seed. Module 1 covers the first seeds in the bin and module 2 does the same, so seeds fill both modules first.
48	- Seeds with the same modules and the same seed data grow as a group. Each seed levels on its own, as it would in its own Powered Planter.
49	- Growth time, power and fertilizer follow ATE's formulas and are read from ATE's live config. Power is drawn each tick for every seed that is still growing. If the power blocks can't cover a planter block's full draw, its seeds stop growing for that tick. Seeds that are already ready still harvest.
50	- Fertilizer is taken from the first non-empty slot of the fertilizer blocks. Each tick, planter blocks claim it in position order, and each group claims one item for every one of its seeds or nothing. A group without a claim grows and harvests unfertilized that tick. A claim uses up fertilizer only when its group harvests, so the fertilizer stored speeds up only as many seeds as it can pay for. A paused group keeps claiming each tick, the way a paused Powered Planter keeps its own fertilizer, so planter blocks later in the order can run unfertilized while it waits.
51	- When there is no room in the export blocks, planter blocks wait. Nothing is voided.
52	- Breaking a block drops everything it holds.
53	- Picking up the whole seed run and putting it back, or scrolling seeds out and back in one at a time, restarts those seeds' growth. No items are lost.
54	
55	### Built-in cloche
56	
57	The core applies a cloche to every planter block. It always works and needs no item. It uses ATE's configured cloche speed and yield bonuses. ATE rounds a 1-item drop at 1.1 yield back to 1, so a cloche does nothing for Mystical Agriculture essence there. The built-in cloche keeps the fraction that rounding throws away and gives one extra item each time it adds up to 1. With the default numbers that is one extra item every tenth harvest.
58	
59	## Recipes
60	
61	These are shaped crafting recipes shipped as datapack JSON, so a pack can replace them.
62	
63	| Block | Pattern | Key |
64	|---|---|---|
65	| Frame | `PPP` `PIP` `PPP` | P = ATE Powered Planter, I = block of iron |
66	| Planter | `FFF` `FIF` `FFF` | F = Frame, I = ATE Infused Farmland |
67	| Core | `IGI` `GCG` `IDI` | C = ATE Cloche Dome, G = glass (`#c:glass_blocks`), I = block of iron, D = block of diamond |
68	| Power | `IRI` `RCR` `IRI` | C = ATE Capacitor Tier 3, R = block of redstone, I = block of iron |
69	| Fertilizer | `IBI` `BSB` `IBI` | S = ATE Fertilizer Spreader, B = bone block, I = block of iron |
70	| Export | `IHI` `HSH` `IHI` | S = ATE Silo, H = hopper, I = block of iron |
71	| ME | `IFI` `FXF` `IFI` | X = any ME Interface (`#ae2:interface`), F = fluix crystal (`#c:gems/fluix`), I = block of iron. Exists only when AE2 is installed. |
72	
73	A planter block costs 8 frames, so 64 Powered Planters plus 8 blocks of iron and one Infused Farmland.
74	
75	## AE2 and Applied Flux
76	
77	The mod runs without AE2, Applied Flux, or both. Without AE2 there is no ME block. Without Applied Flux the ME block does not touch power.
78	
79	### ME block
80	
81	- A multiblock can have at most one ME block. A second one stops the multiblock from forming. The ME block uses one AE2 channel.
82	- Harvests go into ME first and whatever ME does not take goes into the export blocks. When ME is offline (no power or no channel), everything goes to the export blocks.
83	- Every `me_interval` ticks the ME block moves the export blocks' contents into ME and tops the fertilizer blocks up from ME with the fertilizer set in its filter slot.
84	- Item moves cost AE energy, the same as an ME Interface. The ME block also draws 1 AE/t while idle.
85	- The core screen shows the ME status: None, Offline, No channel or Online.
86	
87	### Fertilizer filter
88	
89	The filter slot is a ghost slot. Click it with a fertilizer to set it, or with an empty hand to clear it. Shift-clicking a fertilizer in your inventory also sets it. No item is used up. Only ATE fertilizers are accepted. The top-up fills free room in the fertilizer blocks even when they hold another fertilizer, and the first fertilizer found is still the one planters use.
90	
91	### Applied Flux
92	
93	With Applied Flux installed, the ME block refills the power blocks from ME every tick with what the planter blocks asked for the tick before. That includes planter blocks that paused for power. The refill is capped by free room, so the power blocks are never filled ahead of need.
94	
95	A Flux Accessor placed against the core or a power block also charges it, with or without an ME block.
96	
97	## Logistics Networks
98	
99	Logistics Networks is optional and this mod has no code for it. A node on the core works through the core's connections. The node needs an upgrade sized to the multiblock. A node uses its best upgrade for every channel, and these are Logistics Networks' default limits:
100	
101	| Node upgrade | Energy per tick | Items a second |
102	|---|---|---|
103	| None | 2,000 RF | 0.8 |
104	| Iron | 10,000 RF | 64 |
105	| Gold | 50,000 RF | 256 |
106	| Diamond | 250,000 RF | 5,120 |
107	| Netherite | about 2.1 billion RF | 200,000 |
108	
109	Example with ATE's default numbers: one full planter block of 64 nickel seeds with 2 MK3 Speed Modules, insanium farmland and the built-in cloche.
110	
111	- Power: it draws 32,768 RF/t whatever the seeds' traits.
112	- Items: with seeds that have no traits it puts out about 24 items a second. With seeds maxed in Productive Farming's Growth and Yield it puts out about 320 items a second, which is more than a gold upgrade moves.
113	- Upgrade needed: a diamond upgrade covers up to 7 such planter blocks, and power is the limit. More than 7 needs a netherite upgrade, or more nodes on the power blocks.
114	
115	## Server config
116	
117	| Option | Default | Meaning |
118	|---|---|---|
119	| `part_cap` | 24 | Most parts in one multiblock, not counting the core |
120	| `power_block_buffer` | 4,000,000 | RF each power block holds |
121	| `me_interval` | 20 | Ticks between ME item moves and fertilizer top-ups (1 to 1200) |
122	
123	ATE's numbers are never copied into this config. They are read from ATE.
124	
125	## Build
126	
127	```
128	./gradlew build
129	```
130	
131	The jar is `build/libs/modular_planters-0.1.0.jar`. `./gradlew runGameTestServer` runs the in-game tests.
132	
133	## License
134	
135	MIT, see `LICENSE`. The block textures are adapted from ATE's, which are MIT. ATE's copyright notice is in `LICENSE-ATE.txt` and ships in the jar.

# Modular Planters

A NeoForge addon for Agritech: Evolved (ATE) that replaces many Powered Planters with a few multiblocks. A planter block with N growing seeds produces and draws what N Powered Planters would, and one connection to the core runs the whole multiblock.

It targets Minecraft 26.1.2 and NeoForge 26.1.2.121. ATE 2.2.0 or newer is required. An optional ME block connects a multiblock to an AE2 network, with Applied Flux support. It needs AE2 and does not exist without it.

## Blocks

| Block | Job |
|---|---|
| Core | Forms the multiblock, applies the built-in cloche, opens the core screen, and is the doorway for energy, fertilizer and outputs. It stores nothing itself. |
| Power | Stores energy. Several power blocks pool their storage. Energy goes in but can't be taken out. A broken power block keeps its energy in the dropped item. |
| Fertilizer | 27 slots shared by every planter block. It accepts only ATE fertilizers. |
| Export | 54 slots that hold outputs until something pulls them out. Only the multiblock can insert. Anything can extract. |
| Planter | Grows one seed type, up to 64 seeds. It has a seed slot, a soil slot and two module slots. |
| Frame | Connects parts and does nothing else. |
| ME | Connects the multiblock to an AE2 network. It exists only when AE2 is installed. See AE2 and Applied Flux below. |

Fertilizer and export blocks drop their contents when broken.

### The core as a doorway

While the multiblock is formed, the core exposes two connections:

- Energy inserted into the core goes to the power blocks.
- Items inserted into the core go to the fertilizer blocks, and only fertilizers are accepted. Items extracted from the core come out of the export blocks.

So one Logistics Networks node on the core, or one cable or pipe, runs the whole multiblock. The power, fertilizer and export blocks also expose their own contents directly. While the multiblock is not formed, the core exposes nothing.

### Core screen

The core screen shows the formed state and part count, the reason when the multiblock is not formed, stored power and draw, fertilizer stored, how full the export blocks are, and the ME status. It lists every planter block with its seed, growing count, module coverage, status and position. Each row has an Outline toggle that shows or hides a glowing outline of that block, for you only, and an Open button that opens the planter block's screen remotely. The server checks that you are within 4 blocks of the core and that the planter block belongs to that core's formed multiblock.

## Building rules

- The multiblock is the core plus every part connected to it face to face, directly or through other parts. Diagonal contact does not connect.
- It needs at least one power block, one export block and one planter block. Fertilizer and frame blocks are optional.
- At most 24 parts, not counting the core. Frames count. The cap is in the server config.
- If the connected parts reach a second core, neither core forms. The core screen names the problem block and its position.
- When the shape breaks, planter blocks stop and every block keeps its contents.
- If a connected part is in an unloaded chunk, the multiblock pauses until the chunk loads, and the core screen says so.
- The core can't tell what is in an unloaded chunk, so a multiblock built against the edge of the loaded area also pauses until the next chunk loads, even when no part is in it.

## How a planter block grows

- Growing seeds G is the smaller of the seed count and the soil count. Seeds past that stay idle.
- One module covers one seed. Module 1 covers the first seeds in the bin and module 2 does the same, so seeds fill both modules first.
- Seeds with the same modules and the same seed data grow as a group. Each seed levels on its own, as it would in its own Powered Planter.
- Growth time, power and fertilizer follow ATE's formulas and are read from ATE's live config. Power is drawn each tick for every seed that is still growing. If the power blocks can't cover a planter block's full draw, its seeds stop growing for that tick. Seeds that are already ready still harvest.
- Fertilizer is taken from the first non-empty slot of the fertilizer blocks. Each tick, planter blocks claim it in position order, and each group claims one item for every one of its seeds or nothing. A group without a claim grows and harvests unfertilized that tick. A claim uses up fertilizer only when its group harvests, so the fertilizer stored speeds up only as many seeds as it can pay for. A paused group keeps claiming each tick, the way a paused Powered Planter keeps its own fertilizer, so planter blocks later in the order can run unfertilized while it waits.
- When there is no room in the export blocks, planter blocks wait. Nothing is voided.
- Breaking a block drops everything it holds.
- Picking up the whole seed run and putting it back, or scrolling seeds out and back in one at a time, restarts those seeds' growth. No items are lost.

### Built-in cloche

The core applies a cloche to every planter block. It always works and needs no item. It uses ATE's configured cloche speed and yield bonuses. ATE rounds a 1-item drop at 1.1 yield back to 1, so a cloche does nothing for Mystical Agriculture essence there. The built-in cloche keeps the fraction that rounding throws away and gives one extra item each time it adds up to 1. With the default numbers that is one extra item every tenth harvest.

## Recipes

These are shaped crafting recipes shipped as datapack JSON, so a pack can replace them.

| Block | Pattern | Key |
|---|---|---|
| Frame | `PPP` `PIP` `PPP` | P = ATE Powered Planter, I = block of iron |
| Planter | `FFF` `FIF` `FFF` | F = Frame, I = ATE Infused Farmland |
| Core | `IGI` `GCG` `IDI` | C = ATE Cloche Dome, G = glass (`#c:glass_blocks`), I = block of iron, D = block of diamond |
| Power | `IRI` `RCR` `IRI` | C = ATE Capacitor Tier 3, R = block of redstone, I = block of iron |
| Fertilizer | `IBI` `BSB` `IBI` | S = ATE Fertilizer Spreader, B = bone block, I = block of iron |
| Export | `IHI` `HSH` `IHI` | S = ATE Silo, H = hopper, I = block of iron |
| ME | `IFI` `FXF` `IFI` | X = any ME Interface (`#ae2:interface`), F = fluix crystal (`#c:gems/fluix`), I = block of iron. Exists only when AE2 is installed. |

A planter block costs 8 frames, so 64 Powered Planters plus 8 blocks of iron and one Infused Farmland.

## AE2 and Applied Flux

The mod runs without AE2, Applied Flux, or both. Without AE2 there is no ME block. Without Applied Flux the ME block does not touch power.

### ME block

- A multiblock can have at most one ME block. A second one stops the multiblock from forming. The ME block uses one AE2 channel.
- Harvests go into ME first and whatever ME does not take goes into the export blocks. When ME is offline (no power or no channel), everything goes to the export blocks.
- Every `me_interval` ticks the ME block moves the export blocks' contents into ME and tops the fertilizer blocks up from ME with the fertilizer set in its filter slot.
- Item moves cost AE energy, the same as an ME Interface. The ME block also draws 1 AE/t while idle.
- The core screen shows the ME status: None, Offline, No channel or Online.

### Fertilizer filter

The filter slot is a ghost slot. Click it with a fertilizer to set it, or with an empty hand to clear it. Shift-clicking a fertilizer in your inventory also sets it. No item is used up. Only ATE fertilizers are accepted. The top-up fills free room in the fertilizer blocks even when they hold another fertilizer, and the first fertilizer found is still the one planters use.

### Applied Flux

With Applied Flux installed, the ME block refills the power blocks from ME every tick with what the planter blocks asked for the tick before. That includes planter blocks that paused for power. The refill is capped by free room, so the power blocks are never filled ahead of need.

A Flux Accessor placed against the core or a power block also charges it, with or without an ME block.

## Logistics Networks

Logistics Networks is optional and this mod has no code for it. A node on the core works through the core's connections. The node needs an upgrade sized to the multiblock. A node uses its best upgrade for every channel, and these are Logistics Networks' default limits:

| Node upgrade | Energy per tick | Items a second |
|---|---|---|
| None | 2,000 RF | 0.8 |
| Iron | 10,000 RF | 64 |
| Gold | 50,000 RF | 256 |
| Diamond | 250,000 RF | 5,120 |
| Netherite | about 2.1 billion RF | 200,000 |

Example with ATE's default numbers: one full planter block of 64 nickel seeds with 2 MK3 Speed Modules, insanium farmland and the built-in cloche.

- Power: it draws 32,768 RF/t whatever the seeds' traits.
- Items: with seeds that have no traits it puts out about 24 items a second. With seeds maxed in Productive Farming's Growth and Yield it puts out about 320 items a second, which is more than a gold upgrade moves.
- Upgrade needed: a diamond upgrade covers up to 7 such planter blocks, and power is the limit. More than 7 needs a netherite upgrade, or more nodes on the power blocks.

## Server config

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `part_cap` | 24 | Most parts in one multiblock, not counting the core |
| `power_block_buffer` | 4,000,000 | RF each power block holds |
| `me_interval` | 20 | Ticks between ME item moves and fertilizer top-ups (1 to 1200) |

ATE's numbers are never copied into this config. They are read from ATE.

## Build

```
./gradlew build
```

The jar is `build/libs/modular_planters-0.1.0.jar`. `./gradlew runGameTestServer` runs the in-game tests.

## License

MIT, see `LICENSE`. The block textures are adapted from ATE's, which are MIT. ATE's copyright notice is in `LICENSE-ATE.txt` and ships in the jar.

# Modular Planters Plan 3: Jade and the Guide Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Add the optional Jade tooltips for the core and the planter block, and the Oracle Index guide book with every page the spec lists.

**Architecture:** The Jade data and lines are built by a Jade-free class (`jade/JadeInfo`) that GameTests can call; thin Jade providers wrap it and are only loaded by Jade. The guide is resources only: MDX pages in a top-level `wiki/` folder in the moddedmc.wiki layout, copied into `assets/oracle_index/books/modular_planters` by `processResources`, and checked by JUnit tests that read the folder and the generated recipe JSON.

**Tech Stack:** NeoForge 26.1.2 (ModDevGradle 2.0.141), Java 25, Jade 26.1 API (`snownee.jade.api`), Oracle Index 2.0.0 book format, JUnit 5 with Gson, NeoForge GameTests.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-28-modular-planters-design.md` (sections "Jade" and "Guide"). Plans 1 and 2 are in the same folder. Decisions made without the owner are listed in `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-31-modular-planters-plan-3-todos.md`; the owner confirms them later, and a changed answer becomes a follow-up task.

## Global Constraints

- Platform: NeoForge 26.1.2, Java 25. Mod id `modular_planters`, package `io.github.julianperge.modular_planters`.
- Jade and Oracle Index are optional. The mod has to load and work with either missing. Every GameTest passes with `-PnoJade`.
- Oracle Index needs no code: the guide is resources only, so the build gets no Oracle Index dependency.
- No unicode characters such as em dashes anywhere: code, comments, lang, pages.
- A comment must be necessary (why, cross-file links, intentional absences), a full plain sentence, and complete. Few comments.
- MIT. No code copied from ModularBees. Oritech (`~/DEV/git_repos/minecraft-mods/Oritech`) is the working example for the guide setup and the Jade plugin shape.
- ATE's numbers are never hard-coded in code. Pages may quote ATE's defaults as examples, labeled as defaults, the way the README does.
- `README.md` is the source of truth for player-facing rules; guide pages adapt its sections and must not contradict it.
- Never push. Commit only with the owner's approval for plan 3.
- Subagent prompts that explore code include the project rule: run `graphify query "<question>"` before grep or file reads, and run `graphify update .` after code changes.
- Full verification: `./gradlew test`, `./gradlew runGameTestServer`, and the same GameTests with `-PnoAe2`, `-PnoAppliedFlux` and `-PnoJade`.

## Review Focus

1. A server without Jade and a client with it: the client gets empty server data and must show no lines instead of throwing. Pinned in Task 1 (`emptyServerDataShowsNoLines`).
2. A planter block outside a formed multiblock, or whose core was broken: it must show Idle and 0 growing, not stale numbers. Pinned in Task 1 (`unformedPlanterShowsIdle`).
3. A core before its first scan finishes (Waiting for chunks): it must show the problem, not "Formed". Pinned in Task 1 (`coreShowsItsProblemUntilFormed`).
4. A recipe changed in datagen without the guide page: the page would teach the wrong recipe. Pinned in Task 4 (`blockPagesMatchTheirRecipes`).
5. A `_meta.json` entry or `ModAsset` pointing at a missing file: Oracle Index shows a broken page. Pinned in Task 3 (`metaFilesListEveryPageAndNothingElse`, `everyModAssetExists`).

## File Structure

| Path | Responsibility | Task |
|---|---|---|
| `build.gradle` | Jade `compileOnly` and `localRuntime` (dropped by `-PnoJade`); `processResources` copies `wiki/` | 1, 3 |
| `J/jade/JadeInfo.java` | Jade-free: server data tags and tooltip lines for the core and planter block | 1 |
| `J/jade/MPJadePlugin.java` | `@WailaPlugin` registration | 2 |
| `J/jade/CoreProvider.java`, `J/jade/PlanterProvider.java` | Jade server data and tooltip providers wrapping `JadeInfo` | 2 |
| `J/gametest/JadeTests.java` | GameTests for `JadeInfo` | 1 |
| `J/datagen/MPLang.java` and the generated `en_us.json` | Jade lines and Jade config labels | 1, 2 |
| `wiki/` | The guide book: `sinytra-wiki.json`, `docs/`, `content/`, `assets/` | 3 to 6 |
| `src/test/java/.../wiki/WikiStructureTest.java` | Structure and recipe checks for `wiki/` | 3, 4 |
| `README.md` | Jade and guide sections | 2, 3 |

`J` is `src/main/java/io/github/julianperge/modular_planters`.

---

### Task 1: Jade data and lines without Jade

**Files:**
- Modify: `build.gradle` (dependencies block)
- Create: `J/jade/JadeInfo.java`
- Create: `J/gametest/JadeTests.java`; Modify: `J/gametest/MPTestRegistration.java` (add `JadeTests.register(cases);`)
- Modify: `J/datagen/MPLang.java`, `src/generated/resources/assets/modular_planters/lang/en_us.json`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `CoreBlockEntity.lastScan()` (`ScanResult.formed()`, `partCount()`, `problem()`), `MPConfig.PART_CAP`, `PlanterBlockEntity.status()`, `growing()`, `seeds().size()`.
- Produces, in `io.github.julianperge.modular_planters.jade.JadeInfo` (no Jade imports):
  - `static CompoundTag core(CoreBlockEntity core)`: keys `formed` (boolean), `parts` (int), `cap` (int), `problem` (`Problem` name).
  - `static List<Component> coreLines(CompoundTag data)`
  - `static CompoundTag planter(PlanterBlockEntity planter)`: keys `status` (`PlanterStatus` name), `growing` (int), `seeds` (int).
  - `static List<Component> planterLines(CompoundTag data)`

- [ ] **Step 1: Add Jade to the build**

In `build.gradle` dependencies, next to the AE2 lines:

```groovy
compileOnly "curse.maven:jade-324717:8326300"
if (!project.hasProperty('noJade')) {
    localRuntime "curse.maven:jade-324717:8326300"
}
```

File 8326300 is Jade 26.1.8, the one Oritech builds against; the packs run 26.1.12 (todo item 2).

- [ ] **Step 2: Write the failing GameTests in `JadeTests`**

Register them with `register(Map<String, TestCase> into)` like `MenuTests`, each `new TestCase(20, ...)`, using `Fixtures.rig` and `Fixtures.plant`. Compare components with `helper.assertValueEqual`, since translatable components compare by key and arguments.

```java
// formed_core_shows_its_part_count
CoreBlockEntity core = ...; // a formed rig, after the first scan
List<Component> lines = JadeInfo.coreLines(JadeInfo.core(core));
helper.assertValueEqual(lines, List.of(Component.translatable("modular_planters.jade.formed",
        core.lastScan().partCount(), MPConfig.PART_CAP.get())), "lines");

// core_shows_its_problem_until_formed
// a rig with its power block removed, after a rescan
helper.assertValueEqual(JadeInfo.coreLines(JadeInfo.core(core)), List.of(Component.translatable(
        "modular_planters.jade.not_formed", Component.translatable("modular_planters.problem.missing_power"))), "lines");

// planter_shows_status_and_growing_seeds
Fixtures.plant(planter, 64, 32, 0); // run until the planter has ticked once
helper.assertValueEqual(JadeInfo.planterLines(JadeInfo.planter(planter)), List.of(
        Component.translatable("modular_planters.status.short_on_soil"),
        Component.translatable("modular_planters.jade.growing", 32, 64)), "lines");

// unformed_planter_shows_idle
// a planter block placed alone, with 10 seeds
helper.assertValueEqual(JadeInfo.planterLines(JadeInfo.planter(planter)), List.of(
        Component.translatable("modular_planters.status.idle"),
        Component.translatable("modular_planters.jade.growing", 0, 10)), "lines");

// empty_server_data_shows_no_lines
helper.assertValueEqual(JadeInfo.coreLines(new CompoundTag()), List.of(), "core");
helper.assertValueEqual(JadeInfo.planterLines(new CompoundTag()), List.of(), "planter");
```

- [ ] **Step 3: Run them to see them fail**

Run: `./gradlew runGameTestServer`
Expected: compile failure, `JadeInfo` does not exist.

- [ ] **Step 4: Implement `JadeInfo`**

Problem and status keys are `"modular_planters.problem." + name().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` and `"modular_planters.status." + ...`, the keys the core and planter screens already use. A tag without the `formed` (or `status`) key gives an empty list. Add to `MPLang` and the generated `en_us.json` (keep its alphabetical order, then confirm with `./gradlew runData`):

```
modular_planters.jade.formed      "Formed: %s / %s parts"
modular_planters.jade.not_formed  "Not formed: %s"
modular_planters.jade.growing     "%s/%s seeds growing"
```

- [ ] **Step 5: Run the tests to see them pass**

Run: `./gradlew runGameTestServer` and `./gradlew runGameTestServer -PnoJade`
Expected: all GameTests pass in both runs (125 with Jade; the count rises by the 5 new tests).

- [ ] **Step 6: Commit**

```bash
git add build.gradle src/main/java/io/github/julianperge/modular_planters/jade/JadeInfo.java src/main/java/io/github/julianperge/modular_planters/gametest/JadeTests.java src/main/java/io/github/julianperge/modular_planters/gametest/MPTestRegistration.java src/main/java/io/github/julianperge/modular_planters/datagen/MPLang.java src/generated/resources/assets/modular_planters/lang/en_us.json
git commit -m "feat: build the jade lines for the core and planter block"
```

### Task 2: Jade plugin and providers

**Files:**
- Create: `J/jade/MPJadePlugin.java`, `J/jade/CoreProvider.java`, `J/jade/PlanterProvider.java`
- Modify: `J/datagen/MPLang.java`, the generated `en_us.json`, `README.md`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `JadeInfo` from Task 1; `CoreBlock`, `PlanterBlock`, `CoreBlockEntity`, `PlanterBlockEntity`.
- Produces: `CoreProvider.INSTANCE` and `PlanterProvider.INSTANCE`, enums implementing both `IServerDataProvider<BlockAccessor>` and `IBlockComponentProvider`, with uids `modular_planters:core` and `modular_planters:planter`.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the providers and the plugin**

Follow `Oritech/src/main/java/rearth/oritech/init/compat/jade/`. `appendServerData` copies `JadeInfo.core(...)` (or `planter(...)`) into the given tag when the block entity has the right type; `appendTooltip` adds each line from `JadeInfo.coreLines(accessor.getServerData())`. `MPJadePlugin` is annotated `@WailaPlugin`, registers both data providers against the block entity classes in `register`, and both components against `CoreBlock` and `PlanterBlock` in `registerClient`. Nothing else references these classes, so they load only when Jade does.

Add the Jade config labels to `MPLang` and the generated `en_us.json`:

```
config.jade.plugin_modular_planters.core     "Modular Planters core"
config.jade.plugin_modular_planters.planter  "Modular Planters planter block"
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Verify it compiles and the mod loads with and without Jade**

Run: `./gradlew compileJava runGameTestServer` and `./gradlew runGameTestServer -PnoJade`
Expected: both pass with the same counts as Task 1.

- [ ] **Step 3: Add a "Jade" section to `README.md`**

After "Server config": the core shows "Formed: N / cap parts" or "Not formed: <problem>"; a planter block shows its status and "growing/total seeds growing"; both can be turned off in Jade's plugin settings.

- [ ] **Step 4: Owner check in game**

Run: `./gradlew runClient`. Look at a formed core, an unformed core and a growing planter block. This is added to NOTES.md as an in-game check; the task does not wait for it.

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add src/main/java/io/github/julianperge/modular_planters/jade src/main/java/io/github/julianperge/modular_planters/datagen/MPLang.java src/generated/resources/assets/modular_planters/lang/en_us.json README.md
git commit -m "feat: add the jade plugin for the core and planter block"
```

### Task 3: Guide book setup and structure checks

**Files:**
- Modify: `build.gradle` (`processResources`)
- Create: `wiki/sinytra-wiki.json`, `wiki/docs/_meta.json`, `wiki/docs/overview.mdx`, `wiki/content/_meta.json`
- Create: `src/test/java/io/github/julianperge/modular_planters/wiki/WikiStructureTest.java`
- Modify: `README.md`

**Interfaces:**
- Produces: the `wiki/` layout later tasks add to. Guide pages go in `wiki/docs/`, one page per block in `wiki/content/`, images in `wiki/assets/modular_planters/<folder>/<name>.png`, referenced as `<ModAsset location="modular_planters:<folder>/<name>" width={512} />`.
- Produces: `WikiStructureTest`, which reads `Path.of("wiki")` from the project directory (Gradle's test working directory).

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests**

```java
@Test void wikiIdIsTheModId()          // sinytra-wiki.json "id" equals "modular_planters"
@Test void everyPageHasATitle()        // every .mdx under docs/ and content/ opens with a "---" block holding "title:";
                                       // content/ pages also hold "id: modular_planters:<file name>" and "type: block"
@Test void metaFilesListEveryPageAndNothingElse()
                                       // in every folder under docs/ and content/, the _meta.json keys equal the
                                       // .mdx file names plus the subfolder names
@Test void everyModAssetExists()       // every <ModAsset location="ns:path" in a page has wiki/assets/ns/path.png
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run them to see them fail**

Run: `./gradlew test --tests '*WikiStructureTest'`
Expected: FAIL, `wiki/sinytra-wiki.json` does not exist.

- [ ] **Step 3: Create the book skeleton and copy it into the jar**

`wiki/sinytra-wiki.json`: `{"id": "modular_planters", "schema": "1", "platforms": {}, "owners": ["julian-perge"]}` (todo item 6). `wiki/docs/overview.mdx` with frontmatter `title: Modular Planters` and the README's opening paragraph and "Blocks" list; `docs/_meta.json` lists it as `"overview.mdx": "Overview"`; `content/_meta.json` is `{}` until Task 4. tasks.named('processResources', ProcessResources) {

}
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run the tests and check the jar**

Run: `./gradlew test --tests '*WikiStructureTest' processResources`, then `ls build/resources/main/assets/oracle_index/books/modular_planters`
Expected: tests PASS; the folder holds `sinytra-wiki.json` and `docs/`.

- [ ] **Step 5: Add a "Guide" section to `README.md`**

Before "Build": the in-game guide is an Oracle Index book; the pages live in `wiki/` and are copied into the jar by `processResources`; Oracle Index is optional and the mod has no code for it.

**Files:**
- Create: `wiki/content/{core,frame,planter,power,fertilizer,export,me}.mdx`; Modify: `wiki/content/_meta.json`
- Modify: `WikiStructureTest.java`

- [ ] **Step 3: Write the seven pages**

Frontmatter `id: modular_planters:<block>`, `type: block`, `title: <the block's English name from en_us.json>`. # Plan 3 Todos to Confirm

These are the calls I made while writing plan 3 (`2026-10-31-modular-planters-plan-3-jade-and-guide.md`) instead of asking you. Each one says what the plan does now. Mark each one OK or write what you want instead; a changed answer becomes a follow-up task.

## Jade

1. **What the tooltips show.**
   - Core: "Formed: 12 / 24 parts", or "Not formed: <problem>" using the core screen's problem names.
   - Planter block: its status (Growing, Idle, Short on soil, Paused: ...) and "32/64 seeds growing".
   - Left out: the seed's name, the upgraded count, the ME status, stored power and fertilizer. Add any you want.
2. **Jade version.** The mod compiles against Jade 26.1.8 (CurseForge file 8326300, the one Oritech uses). ATM11 and FTB Evolution 2 both run Jade 26.1.12. The plugin API is the same within 26.1, so this should not matter, but I can pin 26.1.12 if you give me its CurseForge file id or want me to look it up.
3. **Jade in dev runs.** Jade is on the dev runtime (`runClient`, GameTests) the way AE2 is, and `-PnoJade` drops it. The alternative is compile-only, so dev runs never have it.

## Guide

4. **No Oracle Index dependency.** The spec says Oracle Index is `compileOnly`, but the guide has no code, so the build doesn't reference Oracle Index at all. Oritech has the same setup and keeps the dependency only for its own code.
5. **Page layout.**
   - `docs/`: Overview, Building Rules, Example Builds, How a Planter Block Grows, Built-in Cloche, AE2 and Applied Flux, Logistics Networks.
   - `content/`: one page per block, in the order core, planter, power, fertilizer, export, ME, frame.
   - The page text is adapted from README.md, which stays the source of truth.
6. **Book metadata.** `wiki/sinytra-wiki.json` has id `modular_planters`, owner `julian-perge`, and no CurseForge or Modrinth project ids yet, since the mod isn't published. Fill them in when it is.
7. **Tags in recipe pages.** Oritech's recipe pages use only item ids, and I haven't confirmed that Oracle Index accepts tags in a recipe slot. So the pages show one item for each tag:
   - `#c:glass_blocks` as glass;
   - `#ae2:interface` as the ME Interface block;
   - `#c:gems/fluix` as a fluix crystal.
   The ME and core pages also say in words that any glass, or either interface, works.
8. **Example build images.** The three builds are rendered from the canvases in `mockups/layouts.html` with a headless browser (Playwright, which downloads Chromium once), not taken as in-game screenshots. The mockup's fourth card, Trellis, is left out because the spec lists three builds. Swap in in-game screenshots later if you want; the file names stay the same.
9. **English only.** No other languages for the lang keys or the pages.

## Process

10. **Branch.** Plan 3 runs on a new branch, `plan-3-jade-and-guide`, cut from `plan-1-working-multiblock`, the way plan 2 did.
11. **Execution and commits.** I recommend subagent-driven execution, and it needs your commit approval for plan 3. The memory note says to ask again before plan 3 commits.
12. **In-game check.** A Jade check is added to NOTES.md: look at a formed core, an unformed core and a growing planter block. Opening the book in Oracle Index is added too: every page loads, the recipes render, and the three images show.

## Carried over from plan 2

13. **Seed traits.** Very High seeds came out of a planter block whose bin showed lower traits. No cause found in the code. Was more than one planter block or ATE planter feeding the same ME network or chest? If not, a single planter block emptying into an empty chest, with a screenshot of its tooltip, would show it.
14. **In-game checks still open:**
    - shift-click with every slot empty;
    - the seed tooltip cap;
    - the full power bar with Applied Flux;
    - a Flux Accessor charging a power block;
    - the planter screen's fertilizer slot on the client.
15. **Merging into `main`.** `plan-1-working-multiblock` (now 136f695) is still unmerged. Merge before plan 3, after it, or later?
16. **Local leftovers.** `gradle.properties` keeps the uncommitted `neo_version` 26.1.2.116 for ATM11, and `.claude/settings.json.graphify-bak` is untracked. Delete the backup?
17. **README fix.** README.md's Applied Flux section still described the old refill rule. I corrected it on 2026-10-31; it is uncommitted. Commit it on its own, or with plan 3's first commit?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/sweetjp/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-dev/superpowers/7.0.0/skills/subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "executing-plans" [label="yes"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="no"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (inline):**
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution) instead of one context doing every task
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality) instead of only at the end
- Costs a fresh context per task and per review; inline costs one context plus one final reviewer
- Both run in this session, share the same plan workspace and ledger, and never pause between tasks

## The Process

```dot

    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];

        "Fix round R of 5: R≤3 resume implementer; R≥4 fresh implementer, more capable model" [shape=box];

        "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [shape=box];
    }

    "Setup: worktree, ledger check, read plan, pre-flight review" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer (../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)" [shape=box];
    "Final findings? ONE fix dispatch, one scoped re-review, adjudicate residuals" [shape=box];
    "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Setup: worktree, ledger check, read plan, pre-flight review" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer asks questions?";

```

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (under `<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
what you checked as you check it:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.

Write the table to the ledger. Rule on everything you find before execution
begins — each finding against the plan text that mandates it — and record
each ruling in the ledger. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment.
Rule on each conflict it surfaces — the spec is the binding authority, the
plan is its argument — record the ruling beside its row, and dispatch
Task 1. The review loop remains the net for conflicts that only emerge from
implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are
each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix,
constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own
judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
  review seat per task.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, rule on the correction, ledger it, and re-dispatch with the ruling carried in the dispatch

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is yours to rule on: weigh the finding
  against the plan text, decide with the spec as the binding authority, and
  ledger the ruling before you act on it. Do not dismiss the finding because
  the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan
  without a recorded ruling.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — Ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: rule on the smallest change that unblocks the dependent work,
  ledger it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`,
  and carry it into the next task's dispatch. Parking a structural failure
  silently lets every dependent task build on it. Stop only when the defect
  leaves every path forward a guess.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or rule on the load-bearing ones and ledger what you decided. Only
the four classes above stop you here. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing `Ruling:` —
preflight rulings, parked findings, breaker adjudications, all of them — into
your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you made them, each
with what it costs if wrong. The list is exhaustive: if the ledger holds a
ruling, the list holds it. That list is the only place the decisions you
took on your human partner's behalf reach them — they read it and rework
whatever you got wrong. A ruling that dies with the workspace was a decision
made in secret.

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |
| "The implementer spawned its own reviewer — free extra assurance" | It's a duplicate seat reviewing the same diff; the task review is the gate. A worker-spawned reviewer is a defect to flag, not rigor. |

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using Subagent-Driven Development to execute this plan.

[Setup: worktree verified]
[Read plan file once: docs/superpowers/plans/feature-plan.md]
[Resolve workspace: bash scripts/sdd-workspace docs/superpowers/plans/feature-plan.md — no ledger inside, fresh start]
[Create todos for all tasks]

Task 1: Hook installation script

[Run task-brief for Task 1; dispatch implementer with brief + report paths + context]

Implementer: "Before I begin - should the hook be installed at user or system level?"

You: "User level (~/.config/superpowers/hooks/)"

Implementer: [Later]
  - Implemented install-hook command
  - Added tests, 5/5 passing
  - Self-review: Found I missed --force flag, added it
  - Committed

[Run review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD; dispatch task reviewer with the printed path]
Task reviewer: Spec ✅ - all requirements met, nothing extra.
  Strengths: Good test coverage, clean. Issues: None. Task quality: Approved.

[Ledger: Task 1: complete (commits a1b2c3d..d4e5f6a, review clean)]

Task 2: Recovery modes

[Run task-brief for Task 2; dispatch implementer with brief + report paths + context]

Implementer: [No questions]
  - Added verify/repair modes
  - 8/8 tests passing
  - Committed

[Run review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD; dispatch task reviewer with the printed path]
Task reviewer: Spec ❌:
  - Missing: Progress reporting (spec says "report every 100 items")
  Issues (Important): Magic number (100)

[Fix round 1: resume the implementer with both findings]
Implementer: Added progress reporting, extracted PROGRESS_INTERVAL constant.
  Re-ran test/recovery.test.js — 10/10 passing. Fix report appended.

[Run review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD; dispatch scoped re-review]
Re-reviewer: Missing progress reporting — ADDRESSED (src/recovery.js:41).
  Magic number — ADDRESSED (src/recovery.js:7). New breakage: none.
  Verdict: all findings addressed.

[Ledger: Task 2: fix round 1/5 (2 addressed, 0 open; commits d4e5f6a..b7c8d9e)]
[Ledger: Task 2: complete (commits d4e5f6a..b7c8d9e, review clean)]

...

[After all tasks]
[Run review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD; dispatch final code-reviewer, most capable model]
Final reviewer: All requirements met. Deferred minors triaged: none block merge.

[Delete this plan's workspace — the record now lives in git]

Done! Using superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.
```

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## When to Use

```dot

    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [shape=diamond];

    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "executing-plans" [label="yes"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="no"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (inline):**
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution) instead of one context doing every task
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality) instead of only at the end
- Costs a fresh context per task and per review; inline costs one context plus one final reviewer
- Both run in this session, share the same plan workspace and ledger, and never pause between tasks

## The Process
